text.p: An Italian laboratory working on a new test for the banned drug erythropoietin (EPO) has suffered a setback in its research, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) medical commission chief said on Saturday.

Prince Alexandre de Merode said after a two-day meeting in Rome with the heads of 25 IOC accredited laboratories that no date could now be set for a satisfactory urine test being developed in Ferrara by Professor Francesco Conconi.
"I am not setting any date for a result," De Merode said. "We are waiting. Science is not so easy."
De Merode had said in Rome last November that Conconi's research looked like providing a satisfactory solution to tackling a drug considered one of the most dangerous in sport.
He said then that the IOC hoped to be able to validate the method and various procedures involved very soon.
"As I am an optimist, we hope that by the end of the first quarter of next year if all goes well the test could be working in a practical way," De Merode had declared then.
On Saturday, he dampened the optimism.
EPO stimulates the production of red blood cells which transport oxygen around the body -- a quick shot-in-the-arm which replaces high altitude training.
But excessive levels can thicken the blood, resulting in high blood pressure and even heart attacks. The drug is suspected to have killed athletes in the past.
The IOC want to develop a legally binding urine test that distinguishes between internally produced and artificial EPO.

Most banned performance-enhancing drugs can be easily detected through analysis of urine samples. But determining if athletes have taken substances which are also produced naturally in the body is more complicated.

De Merode said that Conconi needed a crucial monoclonal antibody -- cells cultivated in a test tube and narrowly directed towards a specific substance such as EPO -- that could be duplicated repeatedly as the basis for research.
He said Conconi had relied on a laboratory in Genoa to provide such an antibody but all attempts so far had failed to create one that could be sustained and reproduced satisfactorily.
De Merode said such a monoclonal antibody had been created by a research foundation in the United States.
However, that was unavailable because the terms of the U.S. foundation's funding had tight restrictions on its use, forcing the IOC to seek an alternative elsewhere.
De Merode said he was still optimistic that a satisfactory test for EPO could be devised and added that he still felt Conconi's research offered the best hope.
"We are waiting for word from Genoa," he said. "If we can get over this obstacle it (the test) will happen quickly."

Announcing decisions taken during the meeting, De Merode said the IOC medical commission would hold a congress on sports science and education as an alternative to doping to be held in Monte Carlo on October 22-26.
He said a coach from each national Olympic committee would be invited to attend at the IOC's expense. The congress would also be open to athletes and medical staff.
De Merode also said that a $250,000 prize for sports science research would be awarded on January 13 next year in New York.
